cards.title: Worst-case hardness behind circuit learning
cards.formal: Does efficient learning of polynomial-size Boolean circuits imply \(P=NP\)? This is the first of the two unresolved converse implications in the selected source paragraph. Learning uses membership queries and measures error on uniformly random Boolean inputs. The source’s uniformity and resource conventions for “efficient” are not fixed well enough to certify a single formal implication; the remaining choices are described below.

source_formulation.text: However, while some progress on the opposite implications has been made, they remain open, cf. \([2, 33]\).
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

cards.why: Asks whether the difficulty of predicting efficiently computable functions follows from worst-case NP hardness alone. The question probes the gap between worst-case complexity, learning and the average-case hardness used in cryptography; its significance depends on keeping their models and quantifiers distinct.

cards.review_note: The quoted passage leaves two different converse implications open. This card explicitly focuses on efficient learning implying P=NP, while retaining the pseudorandomness alternative as context. The passage describes a randomized learning algorithm but then asks about efficient learning circuits, without fixing uniform versus non-uniform resources for that converse, polynomial resource quantifiers in the target size/error/confidence, or the corresponding uniform complexity conclusion. These choices matter: P=NP, NP contained in BPP, and non-uniform inclusions are different propositions. The full author introduction repeats this wording. Its later precisely parameterized theorem is about provability and does not supply the missing convention for the introductory converse.

sentences: The selected paragraph concerns converses relating circuit learning to P=NP and pseudorandomness.
The principal target here is whether efficient learning forces P=NP.
The learner asks membership queries and must predict well under the uniform distribution.
Reduction barriers and later restricted learning results do not settle that implication.
Uniform versus non-uniform resources and the complete efficiency quantifiers remain to be fixed.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(n\), the unknown target is a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\) computable by a circuit with a polynomial number of gates. Ordinary Boolean circuits may use binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with unbounded fan-out. The notation \(P/\mathrm{poly}\) collects families with some polynomial circuit-size bound; the polynomial may depend on the family.

A membership query consists of the learner choosing any \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) and receiving \(f(x)\). Later queries may depend on earlier answers. The learner is not given a target circuit or the full truth table. Query access permits sampling uniformly random labeled examples as well as asking chosen queries.

The output is an explicitly represented Boolean circuit \(h\) intended to predict the target. For an error parameter \(\varepsilon\) and confidence \(\delta\), the intended guarantee is
\[\Pr_{L}\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_{n}}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq\delta,\]
for every allowed target \(f\), where \(U_{n}\) is uniform on the Boolean cube. The outer probability is over the learner's random bits; the inner one is the prediction error on a fresh uniform input. Here \(\delta\) denotes success confidence, as in the source, not failure probability.

An improper hypothesis may be a larger circuit than the promised target and need not preserve a more restricted target representation. Efficient output still requires an efficient circuit description and evaluation; it does not allow an exponentially long truth table for free. Learning exactly on all inputs, learning under every possible input distribution, and agnostic learning from inconsistent or noisy labels are distinct tasks.

The class \(P\) consists of decision problems solved by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm; \(NP\) consists of those with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in deterministic polynomial time. A randomized learner does not make its proposed consequence automatically \(NP\subseteq BPP\), and a non-uniform learner does not automatically imply a uniform algorithm. These alternatives must not be substituted for the source's stated \(P=NP\) converse without an explicit scope choice.

To complete this card, specify whether one uniform learner is required or polynomial-size oracle circuits may vary non-uniformly with the input length. Also fix the target-size bound supplied to the learner, the polynomial dependence of time or circuit size and query count on that bound and on accuracy/confidence, and the required output-size guarantee. The introductory phrase “small error and high confidence” does not by itself state these quantifiers.

The source separately asks whether the non-existence of strong pseudorandom generators implies efficient learning. That cryptographic converse needs its own stretch, security, uniformity and asymptotic conventions. It is retained as a separate alternative, not conjoined with the principal question here.
cards.answer_criterion: After specifying the outstanding learner conventions, prove or refute the selected implication to P=NP. A theorem about a restricted hypothesis class, a different learning distribution, a different complexity-class conclusion, or the provability of an algorithm in a proof system does not establish this converse. A barrier to a particular kind of reduction also does not refute the implication itself.

context_blocks.title: The known direction and the proposed converse
context_blocks.text: The source records that P=NP supplies efficient learning and asks about reversing this connection. Its main theorem later gives a conditional equivalence between efficiently provable learning and efficiently provable automatability on particular formulas, with changed parameters. That is a different statement.

context_blocks.title: Reduction barriers do not disprove hardness
context_blocks.text: Applebaum, Barak and Xiao show that deriving improper PAC-learning hardness through several natural reduction classes would have major additional consequences. Their principal model is distribution-free PAC learning; its barriers are not an equivalence for the uniform-distribution membership-query model.

context_blocks.title: The cryptographic equivalence has an extra hypothesis
context_blocks.text: Santhanam establishes a learning–one-way-function equivalence under the Universality Conjecture. Keeping that hypothesis is essential; the result does not settle the unconditional converse discussed in the selected paragraph.

context_blocks.title: Later progress preserves meaningful model distinctions
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper obtains results for agnostic semi-proper circuit learning and for other representations, and connects specified reductions to witness encryption. It explicitly distinguishes these from unrestricted improper learning of ordinary Boolean circuits.

cards.context:
The quoted sentence follows the chain from P=NP to efficient circuit learning to failure of strong pseudorandomness. Automatability starts in the next paragraph. The paper’s title therefore did not identify the question selected by this card.

The source records that P=NP supplies efficient learning and asks about reversing this connection. Its main theorem later gives a conditional equivalence between efficiently provable learning and efficiently provable automatability on particular formulas, with changed parameters. That is a different statement.

Applebaum, Barak and Xiao show that deriving improper PAC-learning hardness through several natural reduction classes would have major additional consequences. Their principal model is distribution-free PAC learning; its barriers are not an equivalence for the uniform-distribution membership-query model.

Santhanam establishes a learning–one-way-function equivalence under the Universality Conjecture. Keeping that hypothesis is essential; the result does not settle the unconditional converse discussed in the selected paragraph.

The 2025 paper obtains results for agnostic semi-proper circuit learning and for other representations, and connects specified reductions to witness encryption. It explicitly distinguishes these from unrestricted improper learning of ordinary Boolean circuits.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
